lesson.title: Port Address Translation: One Public Address, Thousands of Connections
lesson.summary: Port address translation extends NAT by rewriting port numbers as well as IP addresses, letting an entire network of devices share a single public IP address at the same time by giving each connection its own unique port on that shared address.
lesson.body:
Plain NAT, as described in the previous chapter, maps one private address to one public address, which means it still needs one public address for every device that wants to be online at the same moment. That does not scale to a household with a dozen internet connected devices sharing one address from an internet provider. Port Address Translation, sometimes called NAT overload or NAPT, solves this by adding port numbers into the translation itself, and it is what almost every home and office router is actually running when people casually refer to it as NAT.

A port number identifies one particular connection or conversation on a given IP address, and PAT exploits this fact directly. Instead of a translation table that only tracks private IP to public IP, a PAT table tracks the full pairing of private IP address and private port number against a public IP address and a public port number the router assigns for that connection. When an internal device opens a new connection, the router picks an available port on its own public address, creates a table entry linking that public port back to the specific private IP and port that originated the connection, and rewrites the outgoing packet accordingly. A reply packet arriving from the internet, addressed to that public port, gets looked up in the table and rewritten back to the correct private IP address and port before being delivered internally.

Consider a small translation table on a router with the single public address 203.0.113.5. A laptop at 192.168.1.10 opens a connection from its local port 51000, and the router maps that to public port 40001. A phone at 192.168.1.11 opens a connection from local port 52222, and the router maps that to public port 40002. The same laptop then opens a second, unrelated connection from local port 53000, and even though it is the same device, the router assigns it a different public port, 40003, because it is a distinct connection. All three entries share the exact same public IP address, 203.0.113.5, and are told apart purely by port number. This is what makes PAT scale: thousands of simultaneous connections can share one public address, because what actually needs to be unique for each connection is the combination of source address, source port, destination address, and destination port, not the address alone.

This is also why an unsolicited connection from the internet cannot normally reach a specific device behind a PAT router without extra configuration such as port forwarding: without an existing table entry created by an outbound connection, the router has no way to know which internal device a stray inbound packet on a public port is meant for.
